numbers.headline: Of 180 adults whose answers showed a likely porn problem, 138 fit the pattern researchers call ‘recovery’ four years later.
numbers.mirror: You think once porn has you, it has you for life.
numbers.counted: adults whose questionnaire answers showed a likely porn or sex problem

basis.design: community group surveyed four times; the researchers’ statistics sorted people into four groups by their 2018 and 2022 answers
basis.who: Jewish adults in Israel aged 18 to 70, men and women together, from a community sample
basis.n: 180: 138 in the group the researchers call ‘recovery’ and 42 in the one they call ‘chronic’ (of 1,182 sorted into four groups)
basis.when: surveys in 2018 and 2022, before the war that began in October 2023, which the later surveys covered; published 2026
basis.measured: Questionnaires for a likely porn problem and a likely compulsive sex problem, at both surveys; the groups count the two together. ‘Recovery’ and ‘chronic’ are the researchers’ names.

numbers.caveat: Questionnaire answers, not a doctor’s check. Men and women are counted together, and so are porn and sex problems; how many were men is not known. ‘Recovery’ is the researchers’ name for a group their statistics drew, so it may not mean each of the 138 is free. Nothing says whether they tried to quit.
numbers.weak: Men and women mixed, and porn and sex problems counted together.

ref.cite: Efrati Y, Shmulewitz D, Skvirsky V, Vider M, Kor A, Lev-Ran S, Mikulincer M (2026). Longitudinal study of probable compulsive sexual behavior disorder and problematic pornography use profiles: their prospective impact on psychopathology during wartime. Addictive Behaviors, article 108589.

was.headline: Across two Israeli surveys, 138 adults fit the pattern the authors call 'recovery' from a porn or sex problem; 42 fit 'chronic'.
was.mirror: You've tried to stop before and think you're stuck with this for good.
was.counted: adults whose questionnaire answers showed a probable porn or sex problem

basis.design: community cohort surveyed four times; people were sorted into groups by a statistical model (latent profile analysis) using the 2018 and 2022 surveys
basis.who: Jewish adults in Israel aged 18 to 70, from a community sample
basis.n: 180 in the two groups whose names say the problem was there in 2018: 138 'recovery' and 42 'chronic' (of 1,182 sorted into four groups)
basis.measured: Self-report questionnaires for probable compulsive sexual behaviour disorder and problem porn use at both surveys. 'Recovery' and 'chronic' are the authors' names for the groups.

was.caveat: Questionnaire scores, not a doctor's diagnosis, and porn and sex problems are counted together. 'Recovery' is the authors' name for a group a model drew; it does not show that each of the 138 dropped below a problem line. The groups rest on the 2018 and 2022 surveys only, so they do not show how people changed or whether it lasted after 2022.
was.weak: How the model drew the 'recovery' group is unchecked, so it may not mean each person got free; how many were men is unknown; porn and sex problems are mixed.

numbers.changeNote: Big figure '138 vs 42' became '138 of 180' (the page shows the share; 'vs' read as two treatments). Headline names a porn problem; the porn-and-sex mix, men and women mixed, and the 'recovery' doubt moved to counted, basis, caveat and weak in plain words. 'Latent profile analysis' replaced by plain words. Basis 'when' explains the 'wartime' title. Mirror rewritten so the number answers it. Source re-fetched: abstract (Europe PMC); full text is open access but the publisher site refused the request, so the 'recovery' definition stays unchecked.

numbers.headline: Of men who wanted help for their porn use, 4 in 10 had already tried to quit four or more times.

numbers.counted: men who said they wanted help for their porn use

basis.who: men who watch porn, found mostly through Craigslist ads; average age 33 among those who wanted help
basis.n: 186 men who wanted help for their porn use (of 1,298 surveyed)
basis.where: USA, Canada and other English-speaking countries
basis.measured: Past tries to quit porn completely and to cut back: none, 1 to 3, or 4 or more. Among men who did not want help, 6% had tried to quit four or more times.

numbers.caveat: One survey at one moment, so it cannot say whether these men got free later or how many tries quitting usually takes. Volunteers who answered an ad.
numbers.weak: Men still struggling, so it can’t show how many tries it took men who got free.

ref.cite: Kraus SW, Martino S, Potenza MN (2016). Clinical characteristics of men interested in seeking treatment for use of pornography. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 5:169-178.
ref.quote: Quit attempts with porn 0 attempts (“never”) 25.3 75.0 251.05 <0.001 1-to-3 past attempts 34.4 19.2 4+ past attempts 40.3 5.8

was.weak: It counts tries so far by men still struggling, not the tries it took men who got free; no porn study counts those.

numbers.changeNote: Mirror rewritten (rule C): 'a fifth is pointless' was confirmed, not answered, by '4 in 10 tried four or more times'; the number does answer 'nobody fails that often'. Weak note cut to one plain reason. Figure, basis and quote unchanged; source re-fetched (Table 1 of the full text: 40.3% of the 186).

numbers.headline: After 12 sessions of ACT, a talk therapy, 54 in 100 men had stopped watching porn completely.
numbers.mirror: You wonder whether therapy can get a man fully off porn.
numbers.counted: men in a therapy trial for problem porn use

basis.design: randomised trial (ACT therapy against a waiting list); this figure counts all men once the waiting-list men had their therapy too
basis.who: adult men with problematic internet porn use; all but one were Latter-day Saints
basis.n: 26 men who finished therapy, both groups together (of 28 who started: 14 given therapy first, 14 on a waiting list)
basis.measured: Self-reported porn viewing at the end of 12 one-to-one sessions of acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), which trains you to let urges come and go without acting on them. While one group waited, viewing fell 93% on average with therapy and 21% on the waiting list.

numbers.caveat: The trial gives no count of men who stopped while on the waiting list, so this is not a with-versus-without figure. There was no comparison therapy, so it does not show ACT beats other help. Three months later, 35 in 100 had stopped completely.
numbers.weak: Only 28 men, almost all from one church.

ref.cite: Crosby JM, Twohig MP (2016). Acceptance and commitment therapy for problematic internet pornography use: a randomized trial. Behavior Therapy 47:355-366.
ref.quote: Complete cessation was seen in 54% of participants at posttreatment and at least a 70% reduction was seen in 93% of participants.

was.headline: In a small trial, men in ACT talk therapy cut porn viewing 93% on average, against 21% on a waiting list.
was.mirror: You've tried willpower alone and want a method that works.

basis.design: randomised trial (ACT therapy vs waiting list)
basis.who: adult men with problematic internet porn use; all but one were Latter-day Saints
basis.n: 28 men: 14 given therapy, 14 on a waiting list; 26 are in the later combined figures
basis.measured: Self-reported porn viewing before and after 12 one-to-one sessions of acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT).

was.caveat: It does not show that ACT beats other therapy: there was no comparison therapy. The 93% was measured at the end of therapy. Once the waiting-list men had therapy too, viewing across all 26 men was down 86% three months later, and 35% had stopped completely.
was.weak: Only 28 men, almost all from one church, and viewing was self-reported.

ref.cite: Crosby JM, Twohig MP (2016). Acceptance and commitment therapy for problematic internet pornography use: a randomized trial. Behavior Therapy 47:355-366.
ref.quote: significant between-condition reductions in pornography viewing compared to the waitlist condition (93% reduction ACT vs. 21% waitlist)

numbers.changeNote: Rule 12a: '93% vs 21%' is a cut in viewing, not people, and read as '93% of men'. Now in people: 54 in 100 men stopped completely after therapy (both groups once treated). The trial reports no people count for the waiting list, so the old '93% vs 21%' wording is kept only in basis.measured and a partial gap note is added for helps-talk. ACT explained in plain words. Weak note kept (28 men). Source re-fetched: abstract on Europe PMC and the USU repository page; full text is behind a paywall.

numbers.headline: Of 104 men keeping an online journal while quitting porn, 55 wrote about slipping at least once.
numbers.mirror: You slipped and think men who really quit never do.
numbers.counted: men on a quit-porn forum, most calling themselves addicted

basis.design: study of online quitting journals, with no comparison group
basis.who: men aged 18 to 63 on the Reboot Nation forum; 80 of the 104 called themselves addicted to porn
basis.measured: Slips the men wrote about, and how long each journal's attempt ran. Only journals covering 7 days to 12 months were picked. At least 86.5% were also trying to stop masturbating.

numbers.caveat: Many men just stopped writing, so nobody knows how their attempts ended, and the study does not say when in an attempt the slips came. Half the journals covered 36.5 days or less. Men who journal in public may differ from men who quit quietly.
numbers.weak: Forum posts from 104 men, with no comparison group.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
ref.quote: More than half of the sample (n = 55) reported at least one lapse during their abstinence attempt.

was.mirror: You broke your streak and think the whole attempt was wasted.
was.weak: A forum sample of 104 men, read from their own posts, with no record of when the slips happened.

numbers.changeNote: Mirror rewritten (rule C): 'the whole attempt was wasted' is not answered by a slip count (the study does not say how the 55 attempts ended); the number does answer 'men who really quit never slip'. Weak note cut to one plain reason. Figure, basis and quote unchanged; source re-fetched.

numbers.weak: Students, mostly women and mostly not hooked, who did not choose to quit.

beliefs.limiting: I’ve watched porn since I was a teenager. It’s wired in. I’m stuck with it.
beliefs.counterpart: Out-of-control porn use often doesn’t last. Plenty of people get past it.
beliefs.test: One evening this week, spend your usual porn hour as a man who got past it would: out, with people, or on something you’ve put off. Before bed, ask whether that man felt like a stranger.
beliefs.proof: In an Israeli survey, 180 adults, men and women, showed a likely porn or sex problem in 2018. By 2022, 138 of them fit the pattern the researchers call ‘recovery’; 42 still fit ‘chronic’.
